meta.title: Test Nation
meta.event: The State of English Cricket — Annual Review 2026

cover.kicker: England and Wales Cricket Board · Annual Review 2026
cover.headline: Test
cover.body: Three years of Bazball. The reinvention of an Ashes rivalry. The quiet revolution in women's cricket. And a question that refuses to go away: what does it mean to play Test cricket in the 21st century?
cover.colophon: Produced by the England and Wales Cricket Board with Harpoon Productions

sections.title: Opening

card_image.alt: England players emerging from the Lord's pavilion

hero_image.alt: Empty Lord's Cricket Ground at dawn, covers on the pitch
hero_image.caption: Lord's Cricket Ground, St John's Wood, London

sections.intro: Test cricket is the longest argument in sport. It began in 1877 and has been revised, challenged, mourned and resurrected in every decade since. What makes this moment different is not the pace at which England are scoring runs — it is the conviction with which they have decided that the game's future depends on making it worth watching again.

pull_quote.text: We don't play Test cricket to survive. We play it to find out what we're made of — and to make it worth two thousand people getting up at 3am on the other side of the world.

sections.title: Bazball

card_image.alt: Zak Crawley driving through the covers

hero_image.alt: England batters running between wickets at pace

sections.intro: The word is a tabloid coinage that became a philosophy. Under Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes, England's Test team adopted a set of principles that sound simple and are extraordinarily difficult to execute: bat without fear, set the pace, never allow the opposition to dictate terms.

sticky_steps.title: Intent
sticky_steps.body: The first principle is non-negotiable: every ball is there to be scored off. This does not mean recklessness — it means that defence is a tactical choice, not a default. England's average first-session scoring rate since 2022 is 4.3 runs per over, compared to a global Test average of 3.1.

image.alt: Zak Crawley pulls a short ball over midwicket

sticky_steps.title: Trust
sticky_steps.body: McCullum's signal achievement has been convincing players that failure is not career-ending. England's top-order batters average more than 50 balls faced before they are dismissed — a higher average than at any point in the previous decade — but they are also dismissed more often for scores below 20. The trust cuts both ways.

image.alt: McCullum and Stokes in conversation at the crease

sticky_steps.title: The Chases
sticky_steps.body: The statistical hallmark of the Stokes era is England's fourth-innings record. They have successfully chased 21 targets in 30 attempts since June 2022 — a conversion rate of 70%, compared to a global Test average of 41%. Three of those chases exceeded 350 runs, a figure previously achieved only once in Test history.

image.alt: England players on the balcony watching the final overs of a chase

sticky_steps.title: The Limits
sticky_steps.body: Bazball has not been universally successful. On rank-turning pitches in South Asia, the approach requires modification that has not always been convincingly made. The 2025 tour of India — lost 3–1 — exposed the limits of aggressive intent against world-class spin on home pitches. The question of adaptability remains open.

image.alt: England spinner bowling in subcontinental conditions

hero_image.alt: The urn held aloft at Lord's at close of play on the final day

pull_quote.text: There is no series in world cricket that carries this weight. We never stop being aware of it, and we never stop pretending that we aren't.

sections.title: The Ashes 2025

card_image.alt: The Ashes urn on display at Lord's

sections.intro: England retained the Ashes in 2025, winning the series 3–1 with a match to spare. It was the first time England had retained the urn in successive series since 1986–87. These are the five Tests that defined the summer.

cards.title: First Test · Headingley · England won by 9 wickets
cards.body: England's Ollie Pope scored 196 on the first day — the highest score by an England batter at Headingley since Len Hutton's 202 in 1939. Australia were bowled out for 147 in their second innings as Mark Wood took 5–32 at 95mph.

image.alt: Ollie Pope drives through the covers at Headingley

cards.title: Second Test · Lord's · Australia won by 43 runs
cards.body: Australia's Pat Cummins was magnificent in both innings, taking nine wickets in the match. England, set 271 to win, were bowled out for 227 in the final session as Nathan Lyon turned the ball sharply on a deteriorating surface.

image.alt: Pat Cummins celebrates a wicket at Lord's

cards.title: Third Test · Edgbaston · England won by an innings and 47 runs
cards.body: The decisive match of the series. Joe Root scored 262 — his highest Test score — in a first-innings total of 657. Australia never recovered. England's Gus Atkinson took ten wickets in the match on his home ground.

image.alt: Joe Root raises his bat after reaching 250 at Edgbaston

cards.title: Fourth Test · Old Trafford · England won by 5 wickets
cards.body: England retained the Ashes with a Test to spare. Ben Stokes, under the floodlights of a sold-out Old Trafford, hit the winning runs in the final over. It was his first fifty of the series. The crowd were still singing at midnight.

image.alt: Ben Stokes hits the winning six at Old Trafford

crossfade_images.alt: Ground staff removing covers at dawn, heavy dew on the outfield
Full ground at evening, long shadows across the outfield

crossfade_phases.text: A Test match begins before a ball is bowled — in the decisions about the pitch, the weather, the squad, the toss.
It ends, five days later, with something that could not have been predicted from the first morning's play. That is why we come back.

sections.title: The Women's Game

hero_image.alt: Nat Sciver-Brunt drives through the off side

sections.intro: England Women have won successive Ashes series, a World T20 title and a first women's Test at Lord's in forty years. They are no longer the secondary story. They are, in many respects, the more interesting one.

toggle_panels.label: Test Cricket
toggle_panels.body: England Women played four Test matches in 2025 — more than in any year since 1998. The return of multi-Test series, including the first women's Test at Lord's since 1984, represents a structural commitment to the long form of the women's game that was previously absent. Attendance at the Lord's Test was 22,000 across four days.

image.alt: England Women at Lord's, women's Test, 2025

toggle_panels.label: T20 World Cup
toggle_panels.body: England Women won the ICC T20 World Cup in Bangladesh in October 2025, defeating Australia in the final by 8 runs. It was England's first global women's title since the 2009 T20 World Cup. Sophie Ecclestone was named Player of the Tournament after taking 17 wickets at an average of 8.2.

image.alt: England Women lift the T20 World Cup

toggle_panels.label: Participation
toggle_panels.body: Recreational women's and girls' cricket participation reached 460,000 registered players in 2025 — a 34% increase since 2022. The ECB's Dynamos Cricket programme now reaches 180,000 girls aged 8–11 annually. The pipeline from grassroots to county to international is, for the first time, genuinely continuous.

image.alt: Girls in a Dynamos Cricket session

images.caption: Nat Sciver-Brunt: 847 runs and 24 wickets in 2025

images.alt: Sophie Ecclestone in her delivery stride
images.caption: Sophie Ecclestone: world's number one ranked women's bowler

sections.title: The County Game

card_image.alt: A county ground on a sunny afternoon, sparse crowd

hero_image.alt: Trent Bridge on a quiet county championship morning

sections.intro: The County Championship is the engine room of English cricket. It is also its most contested institution — perpetually debated, restructured and defended. The 2025 season produced the closest title race in twenty years.

accordion_items.title: Surrey — County Champions 2025

thumbnail.alt: Surrey lift the County Championship pennant

accordion_items.body: Surrey won the County Championship for the third time in four seasons, confirming their position as the dominant county side of the mid-2020s. Their success has been built on an exceptional pace attack — Atkinson, Overton and Clarke took 187 Championship wickets between them — allied to the reliable batting of Rory Burns, who scored 1,412 runs in the season at an average of 58.

pull_quote.text: We don't talk about legacy at Surrey. We talk about what we're doing tomorrow.

stats.label: Rory Burns: runs in the Championship season

accordion_items.title: Lancashire — Runners-Up

thumbnail.alt: Lancashire players in the field at Emirates Old Trafford

accordion_items.body: Lancashire pushed Surrey to the final week of the season, ultimately finishing four points behind. Their top-order batting — anchored by Keaton Jennings and the emerging Josh Bohannon — was the strongest in the division. Lancashire's failure to win the Championship has become one of county cricket's recurring narratives; they have finished second or third in six of the past ten seasons.

stats.label: Points separating Surrey and Lancashire at the final reckoning

accordion_items.title: Derbyshire — Promoted from Division Two
accordion_items.body: Derbyshire's promotion from Division Two was the story of the domestic season. Under new head coach Andy Hurry, they developed three England-qualified seamers under 23 and won nine of their fourteen Championship matches. Their return to the top flight after four seasons away was comfortable and convincing.

sections.title: Voices of the Game
sections.intro: The people who shaped English cricket in 2025.

contributors.name: Ben Stokes
contributors.title: England Test Captain
contributors.bio: In three years as captain, Ben Stokes has transformed England's Test team from a demoralised group finishing the 2021–22 Ashes without a win to the most watchable Test side in the world. His own performances — 847 runs and 34 wickets in 2025 — suggest that the captaincy has liberated rather than burdened him.

contributors.name: Brendon McCullum
contributors.title: England Test Head Coach
contributors.bio: The New Zealander brought to English cricket something it had spent thirty years trying to manufacture: genuine fearlessness. His coaching philosophy — outlined in the now-famous 'Headingley meeting' of June 2022 — has become a case study in sports leadership internationally.

contributors.name: Nat Sciver-Brunt
contributors.title: England Women's Captain
contributors.bio: The finest all-round cricketer England have produced in a generation, Nat Sciver-Brunt leads the women's team with the same combination of authority and warmth that defines her batting. Her return from a period of mental health leave in 2023 has been one of sport's more remarkable comebacks.
